Apple___Apple_scab.description: A common fungal disease of apple that causes dark scabby lesions on leaves and fruit, reducing yield and fruit quality.
symptoms: Olive-green to dark brown velvety spots on leaves
Leaves may curl, yellow and drop early
Corky, cracked dark lesions on fruit
causes: Fungus overwinters in fallen infected leaves
Spores spread by rain splash and wind in cool, wet spring weather
prevention: Rake and destroy fallen leaves in autumn
Plant scab-resistant varieties
Prune to open the canopy for faster drying
treatment: Apply protective fungicides (e.g. captan, mancozeb or sulfur) from green-tip through petal fall
Follow local extension spray schedules and label directions

Apple___Black_rot.description: Fungal disease causing leaf spots, fruit rot and limb cankers on apple trees.
symptoms: Purple spots on leaves that enlarge into 'frog-eye' lesions with tan centres
Rotting fruit with concentric dark rings, later mummified
Sunken reddish-brown cankers on branches
causes: Fungus survives in mummified fruit, dead wood and cankers
Spread by rain splash during warm, wet weather
prevention: Remove mummified fruit and prune out dead or cankered wood
Keep trees vigorous and avoid wounding bark
Clean up orchard debris
treatment: Prune cankers well below visible infection
Apply fungicides such as captan during the growing season as recommended locally

Apple___Cedar_apple_rust.description: A rust disease that needs both apple and juniper/red cedar hosts to complete its life cycle.
symptoms: Bright yellow-orange spots on upper leaf surface
Small tube-like structures on leaf undersides later in the season
Premature leaf drop and deformed fruit in severe cases
causes: Spores released from galls on nearby juniper/cedar trees in wet spring weather
prevention: Plant rust-resistant apple varieties
Remove nearby junipers/red cedars or their galls where practical
treatment: Apply protective fungicides (e.g. myclobutanil, mancozeb) from pink bud through early summer per label

Apple___healthy.description: The apple leaf shows no visible signs of the diseases this model recognises.
symptoms: Uniform green colour
No spots, lesions, mould or abnormal curling
prevention: Keep monitoring plants weekly, especially after rain or humid spells
Water at the base of the plant and avoid wetting foliage
Maintain good spacing and airflow; remove weeds and plant debris
Use balanced fertilisation and disease-free planting material
treatment: No treatment needed

Cherry_(including_sour)___Powdery_mildew.description: Fungal disease forming white powdery growth on cherry leaves and shoots, weakening trees.
symptoms: White powdery patches on leaves and young shoots
Leaves curl upward and may become distorted
Fruit may show a faint white coating
causes: Warm days, cool nights and high humidity
Spores spread by wind; does not need free water
prevention: Prune for good airflow and sunlight penetration
Avoid excess nitrogen fertilisation
Remove root suckers and water sprouts
treatment: Apply sulfur or other labelled fungicides at first sign of disease
Repeat applications as directed during favourable weather

Corn_(maize)___Cercospora_leaf_spot Gray.description: One of the most yield-limiting foliar diseases of maize in warm, humid regions.
symptoms: Narrow rectangular grey to tan lesions running parallel to leaf veins
Lesions merge and blight whole leaves
Lower leaves affected first
causes: Fungus survives on infected corn residue
Favoured by prolonged leaf wetness, high humidity and warm temperatures
prevention: Use resistant hybrids
Rotate crops away from corn for at least one year
Bury or manage crop residue
treatment: Apply foliar fungicides (e.g. strobilurins, triazoles) at disease onset on susceptible hybrids per local advice

Corn_(maize)___Common_rust_.description: A rust disease producing powdery reddish-brown pustules on maize leaves.
symptoms: Small, elongated cinnamon-brown pustules on both leaf surfaces
Pustules rupture releasing rusty powder
Severe cases cause leaf yellowing and death
causes: Wind-blown spores, often from distant regions
Cool temperatures (16–23 °C) with heavy dew or humidity
prevention: Plant resistant hybrids
Plant early to avoid peak spore periods
treatment: Fungicide application is warranted on susceptible sweet corn or seed corn when pustules appear early

Corn_(maize)___Northern_Leaf_Blight.description: Fungal leaf disease producing long cigar-shaped lesions that can cause significant yield loss.
symptoms: Long (2.5–15 cm) elliptical grey-green to tan lesions
Lesions start on lower leaves and progress upward
Dark spore masses in lesions in humid weather
causes: Fungus overwinters on corn residue
Moderate temperatures (18–27 °C) and long dew periods
prevention: Use resistant hybrids
Crop rotation and residue management
treatment: Apply foliar fungicides at early tasseling if disease appears on upper leaves of susceptible hybrids

Grape___Black_rot.description: A destructive fungal disease of grapes that can destroy an entire crop in warm, wet seasons.
symptoms: Small brown circular leaf spots with dark borders and black dots
Berries turn brown, then shrivel into hard black mummies
Lesions on shoots and tendrils
causes: Fungus overwinters in mummified berries and canes
Spread by rain during warm, wet weather
prevention: Remove mummies and infected canes during dormant pruning
Improve canopy airflow
Control weeds under vines
treatment: Apply protective fungicides (e.g. mancozeb, myclobutanil) from bud break through berry set per label

Grape___Esca_(Black_Measles).description: A grapevine trunk disease complex that causes leaf discoloration, berry spotting and vine decline.
symptoms: 'Tiger-stripe' pattern: yellow or red areas between veins that dry out
Small dark spots on berries
Sudden wilting and death of vines (apoplexy)
causes: Wood-infecting fungi entering through pruning wounds
prevention: Prune during dry weather and protect large pruning wounds
Remove and destroy dead or infected wood
Use clean nursery stock
treatment: No curative chemical treatment; remove infected arms/trunks and retrain new shoots
Wound protectants can reduce new infections

Grape___Leaf_blight_(Isariopsis_Leaf_Spo.description: Fungal leaf spot disease of grapes that can cause premature defoliation.
symptoms: Irregular dark red-brown to black spots on leaves
Spots enlarge and merge; leaves dry and drop
Mostly affects older leaves
causes: Warm, humid conditions
Spores spread by wind and rain from infected leaves
prevention: Remove fallen infected leaves
Improve canopy ventilation
Avoid overhead irrigation
treatment: Apply copper-based or other labelled fungicides when disease is first observed

Orange___Haunglongbing_(Citrus_greening).pathogen: Candidatus Liberibacter spp. (bacterium), spread by Asian citrus psyllid
Orange___Haunglongbing_(Citrus_greening).description: A devastating, incurable bacterial disease of citrus that causes tree decline and bitter, misshapen fruit.
symptoms: Blotchy, asymmetric yellow mottling of leaves
Small, lopsided, bitter fruit that stay green at the bottom
Twig dieback and overall decline
causes: Bacterium transmitted by the Asian citrus psyllid
Spread via infected budwood or nursery plants
prevention: Use certified disease-free nursery trees
Monitor and control psyllid populations
Report suspected cases to local agricultural authorities
treatment: No cure; remove and destroy infected trees to protect healthy ones
Nutritional sprays can prolong productivity but do not cure

Peach___Bacterial_spot.description: Bacterial disease causing leaf spots, defoliation and fruit blemishes on peach and other stone fruits.
symptoms: Small water-soaked spots on leaves that turn purple-brown and fall out ('shot-hole')
Yellowing and early leaf drop
Sunken pits and cracks on fruit
causes: Bacteria overwinter in twig cankers
Spread by wind-driven rain; favoured by warm, wet weather
prevention: Plant resistant varieties
Avoid excessive nitrogen
Site orchards with good air movement
treatment: Apply copper sprays during dormancy and oxytetracycline or labelled bactericides in season per local guidance

Pepper,_bell___Bacterial_spot.description: A bacterial disease causing leaf spots and fruit lesions on pepper, common in warm, wet climates.
symptoms: Small water-soaked leaf spots that turn brown with yellow halos
Leaf yellowing and drop
Raised scabby spots on fruit
causes: Infected seed or transplants
Spread by splashing water, tools and handling wet plants
prevention: Use certified disease-free seed and transplants
Rotate crops (2–3 years away from peppers/tomatoes)
Avoid overhead irrigation and working with wet plants
treatment: Apply copper-based bactericides (often with mancozeb) preventively
Remove severely infected plants

Potato___Early_blight.description: A common fungal disease of potato and tomato causing target-like leaf spots and yield loss.
symptoms: Dark brown spots with concentric rings ('target' pattern) on older leaves
Yellowing around spots
Lesions can occur on stems and tubers
causes: Fungus survives in soil and plant debris
Warm temperatures with alternating wet and dry periods; stressed plants
prevention: Rotate crops
Use certified seed tubers
Maintain adequate fertility and irrigation to reduce plant stress
treatment: Apply fungicides such as chlorothalonil or mancozeb when first symptoms appear, repeating per label

Potato___Late_blight.description: A highly destructive disease (cause of the Irish potato famine) that can destroy fields within days.
symptoms: Large, dark, water-soaked lesions on leaves, often starting at tips/edges
White fuzzy growth on leaf undersides in humid conditions
Brown, firm rot of tubers
causes: Spread by airborne spores in cool, wet weather
Infected seed tubers and volunteer plants
prevention: Use certified disease-free seed
Destroy cull piles and volunteer potatoes
Plant resistant varieties; hill soil over tubers
treatment: Apply protectant/systemic fungicides (e.g. chlorothalonil, mancozeb, cymoxanil) promptly
Remove and destroy infected plants; harvest only after vines are dead

Squash___Powdery_mildew.description: A very common fungal disease of cucurbits that reduces photosynthesis and fruit quality.
symptoms: White powdery spots on upper and lower leaf surfaces
Spots spread to cover entire leaves
Leaves yellow, wither and die early
causes: Warm, dry days with humid nights
Dense planting and shade; wind-borne spores
prevention: Plant resistant varieties
Space plants for good airflow and full sun
Remove infected leaves early
treatment: Apply sulfur, potassium bicarbonate, neem oil or labelled fungicides at first sign

Strawberry___Leaf_scorch.description: Fungal leaf disease of strawberry that weakens plants and reduces next season's yield.
symptoms: Numerous small irregular purple spots on upper leaf surface
Spots merge; leaf appears scorched and dries
No distinct light centres (unlike leaf spot)
causes: Fungus overwinters on infected leaves
Spread by splashing water in warm, wet weather
prevention: Use disease-free transplants and resistant varieties
Renovate beds and remove old leaves after harvest
Avoid overhead irrigation
treatment: Apply labelled fungicides (e.g. captan) from early spring through harvest per local guidance

Tomato___Bacterial_spot.description: Bacterial disease of tomato causing leaf spots, defoliation and scabby fruit.
symptoms: Small dark water-soaked spots on leaves, sometimes with yellow halos
Spots become greasy then dry and may fall out
Raised brown scabby spots on fruit
causes: Infected seed and transplants
Splashing rain, overhead irrigation, handling wet plants
prevention: Use disease-free seed and transplants
Rotate crops; remove debris
Avoid overhead watering
treatment: Apply copper-based bactericides preventively, often combined with mancozeb
Remove heavily infected plants

Tomato___Early_blight.description: Common fungal disease of tomato producing target-like spots and defoliation from the bottom up.
symptoms: Brown spots with concentric rings on older, lower leaves
Yellowing around lesions and leaf drop
Dark sunken lesions at the stem end of fruit
causes: Fungus survives in soil and debris
Warm, humid weather; stressed or older plants
prevention: Mulch to prevent soil splash
Stake and prune for airflow
Rotate crops for 2–3 years
treatment: Remove infected lower leaves
Apply fungicides such as chlorothalonil, mancozeb or copper per label

Tomato___Late_blight.description: Fast-spreading, destructive disease of tomato and potato in cool, wet weather.
symptoms: Large greasy grey-green to brown blotches on leaves
White mould on leaf undersides in humid conditions
Firm brown greasy patches on fruit
causes: Airborne spores from infected tomato/potato plants
Cool (10–24 °C), wet, humid conditions
prevention: Plant resistant varieties
Avoid overhead irrigation; space plants well
Remove volunteer potatoes and tomatoes
treatment: Apply fungicides (e.g. chlorothalonil, mancozeb, copper) preventively during risk periods
Remove and bag infected plants immediately; do not compost

Tomato___Leaf_Mold.description: Fungal disease mostly of greenhouse or high-humidity tomatoes.
symptoms: Pale green to yellow spots on upper leaf surface
Olive-green to brown velvety mould on undersides
Leaves curl, wither and drop
causes: High relative humidity (>85%) and poor ventilation
Spores survive on debris and greenhouse structures
prevention: Improve ventilation and reduce humidity
Space and prune plants
Use resistant varieties
treatment: Remove infected leaves
Apply labelled fungicides (e.g. chlorothalonil, copper) if humidity cannot be controlled

Tomato___Septoria_leaf_spot.description: Very common fungal disease causing numerous small leaf spots and severe defoliation.
symptoms: Many small circular spots with dark borders and grey/tan centres
Tiny black dots (fruiting bodies) in spot centres
Lower leaves yellow and drop first
causes: Fungus survives on debris and solanaceous weeds
Spread by water splash in warm, wet weather
prevention: Rotate crops and remove debris
Mulch and water at the base
Control nightshade weeds
treatment: Remove infected leaves
Apply chlorothalonil, mancozeb or copper fungicides per label

Tomato___Spider_mites Two-spotted_spider.description: Tiny sap-sucking mites that cause stippling and bronzing of tomato leaves, worst in hot, dry weather.
symptoms: Fine yellow or white speckling (stippling) on leaves
Leaves bronze, dry and drop
Fine webbing on leaf undersides
causes: Hot, dry, dusty conditions
Overuse of broad-spectrum insecticides that kill natural predators
prevention: Keep plants well watered; reduce dust
Encourage natural predators (predatory mites, ladybirds)
Inspect leaf undersides regularly
treatment: Spray leaves with water to dislodge mites
Apply insecticidal soap, horticultural oil, neem or labelled miticides

Tomato___Target_Spot.description: Fungal disease causing target-like lesions on tomato leaves, stems and fruit in warm, humid climates.
symptoms: Brown spots with concentric rings and yellow halos on leaves
Lesions merge causing leaf blight
Sunken spots on fruit
causes: Warm (20–28 °C), humid conditions with long leaf wetness
Fungus survives on crop debris
prevention: Improve airflow through pruning and spacing
Avoid overhead irrigation
Rotate crops and remove debris
treatment: Apply labelled fungicides (e.g. chlorothalonil, azoxystrobin) when symptoms appear

Tomato___Tomato_Yellow_Leaf_Curl_Virus.description: A serious viral disease transmitted by whiteflies that stunts plants and severely reduces yield.
symptoms: Upward curling and cupping of leaves
Yellow leaf margins
Stunted growth and flower drop
causes: Transmitted by the silverleaf whitefly (Bemisia tabaci)
Infected transplants
prevention: Use resistant varieties and virus-free transplants
Control whiteflies with nets, reflective mulches and traps
Remove weeds that host whiteflies
treatment: No cure; remove and destroy infected plants
Manage whitefly populations to limit spread

Tomato___Tomato_mosaic_virus.description: A highly contagious virus spread mechanically by hands, tools and seed.
symptoms: Light and dark green mosaic pattern on leaves
Leaf distortion and fern-like leaves
Stunted plants and uneven fruit ripening
causes: Contaminated seed, tools, hands and plant debris
Very stable virus that survives long periods
prevention: Use certified virus-free seed and resistant varieties
Disinfect tools and wash hands; avoid tobacco use near plants
Remove infected plants and debris
treatment: No cure; remove and destroy infected plants
Sanitise equipment to prevent spread
